notes.meaning: Peter speaks directly to the elders, the leaders in the local churches, describing himself as a fellow elder. He saw Christ's sufferings firsthand and shares in the promise of the coming heavenly glory. Instead of giving orders as an apostle, he gently urges these leaders to care well for their people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Peter calls himself a fellow elder out of personal humility, which does not take away his unique role as the head of the apostles.

notes.meaning: Church leaders are called to care for God's people just as a shepherd watches over sheep. They should serve willingly because they love God, not because someone makes them do it. Their motivation must be an eager heart to help others, rather than a desire to make money or gain power.

Pastors must not act like harsh bosses over the believers in their care. The church belongs to God, not to the leaders. Leaders should guide people by living out a good example for the whole flock to follow.

differ.view: Church leaders have lawful governing authority over their people as rulers, but they are forbidden to abuse that role by acting like tyrants.
The word for God's heritage belongs to all church members equally, meaning pastors have no special priestly rank to rule over others.

notes.meaning: Jesus is the Chief Shepherd who owns and cares for all his people. When he returns, faithful leaders will receive an unfading crown of glory. Unlike athlete wreaths in the ancient world that quickly dried up, the reward Christ gives will never perish.

Younger believers are told to respect and follow the guidance of older church leaders. Beyond that, every Christian must serve others with genuine humility, like tying on a servant's apron. Scripture warns that God stands against the proud, but he freely pours out his grace on the humble.

Believers are told to submit quietly under God's powerful hand during painful trials. Trusting his mighty control keeps people from acting out in pride or bitterness. When the right moment arrives, God himself will lift up those who remain humble.

Christians are encouraged to throw all their worries and fears onto God. He cares deeply about everything that affects his children, both big and small. Leaving our burdens in his hands frees our minds from anxiety.

Believers need to keep a clear head and stay wide awake. The devil is a fierce enemy who stalks around like a hungry, roaring lion looking for someone to destroy. Christians must never let down their spiritual guard against his attacks.

Christians must stand their ground against the devil by holding firmly to their faith in God. They can find courage in knowing that other believers across the world are facing the exact same trials. No Christian suffers alone in the fight against evil.

Earthly suffering lasts only a short time compared to eternity. God, who provides grace—his free gift of love and help—has called believers to share in his everlasting glory through Christ. After their trials, God will personally mend, support, strengthen, and firmly settle his people.

differ.view: "Perfect" means God completing his work of grace in us, so that no weakness or defect remains.
"Perfect" means growing in holiness little by little. Even the best believers are not fully perfect in this life.

notes.meaning: Peter ends his encouraging words with a burst of praise to God. He declares that all ruling power belongs to God forever. Christians can find deep peace knowing that their Lord holds complete control over all things.

Peter sent this letter with Silvanus, also called Silas, whom he trusted as a dependable Christian brother. His goal was to comfort the readers and assure them that the gospel they heard is the true grace of God. He urges them to keep standing strong in this truth.

The believers send warm greetings from the church in Babylon, which was a code name for the mighty Roman capital. Mark, whom Peter loves like a son in the faith, sends his greetings as well. Even living in a world hostile to God, his chosen people remain united.

differ.view: "Babylon" means the real city of Babylon, where many Jews lived. Peter, as apostle to the Jews, would naturally go there.
"Babylon" is a code name for Rome. It fits the letter's picture of Christians as exiles far from home.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Babylon is a symbolic name for the city of Rome, which shows that Peter lived and ministered in Rome before his death.

notes.meaning: The letter closes with an appeal for believers to greet one another with a sincere kiss of Christian love. This customary greeting showed their pure family bond and unity in the Lord. Peter finishes by praying that Christ's peace will rest on all who belong to him.
